messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas, a 26-year-old detective married to his partner for two years, sought help after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms following an incident of physical abuse by his romantic partner. The trauma has deeply affected Thomas’s daily life and work as a detective, leading him to avoid situations that could trigger painful memories. On the night of the traumatic event, Thomas was home when his partner became aggressive after drinking heavily. The alcohol smell now triggers intense nausea for Thomas whenever he encounters it, making social gatherings at work unbearable. This olfactory trigger not only induces physical distress but also immerses him in vivid auditory and visual recollections of that fateful night. He hears the sounds of breaking glass and sees his own bruised face reflected in a shattered mirror — memories so clear they force their way into his mind unbidden, even when he tries to focus on work. The triggers not only intensify his memory recall but also reinforce Thomas’s negative appraisals about himself and others. He has lost faith in people and life itself, feeling permanently like an outsider who cannot trust anyone around him. These beliefs have deepened over time as the vivid memories of the abuse continue to surface, making it increasingly difficult for him to engage with his environment. Thomas’s maladaptive strategies are a direct response to these persistent triggers and intrusive memories. He avoids relaxing because doing so makes him feel vulnerable and in danger. This constant state of vigilance leads him to numb his feelings, leaving him emotionally detached from both work and personal relationships. The physical contact avoidance extends beyond intimate touch to any form of physical contact with colleagues or friends, leading to strained interactions at the precinct. The weight of these negative appraisals has compounded Thomas’s maladaptive strategies, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. He believes that people are not what they seem, and this distrust makes him wary of forming close bonds, which in turn reinforces his feelings of isolation and fear. The avoidance behaviors have also led to tangible consequences at work; he now struggles to collaborate effectively with colleagues, affecting both his job performance and the quality of his investigations. What finally brought Thomas to seek help was a particularly distressing encounter at a crime scene where he saw visible injuries on a victim that mirrored his own from the past. This trigger not only sent him spiraling into intense nausea but also flooded him with vivid memories of the abuse, making it impossible for him to continue working on the case. In this moment, Thomas realized that he needed professional support to navigate these overwhelming feelings and regain control over his life. Thomas is most afraid of remaining trapped in a cycle of avoidance and mistrust, unable to form genuine connections or perform his job with integrity. He hopes that therapy will help him process the trauma, rebuild trust, and find ways to relax without feeling like he’s endangering himself.
